title: Mechanisms of Neural Stem Cell Mechanoregulation
text:
Adult neural stem cells (NSCs) are a population of cells in the adult brain that can self-renew and give rise to a
variety of cell types, including neurons. NSCs are of tremendous interest for both their potential role in neural
development and disease and because they may be harnessed in various ways to treat neurodegenerative
disease (e.g., Alzheimer’s, Parkinson’s, and Lou Gehrig’s Diseases). The goal of this proposal is to understand
mechanisms through which biomechanical inputs from the cellular microenvironment influence NSC
neurogenesis, which we expect will significantly add to our understanding of NSC biology and help inform the
design of tissue engineering and regenerative medicine strategies to treat disease.

title: Developing a gene therapy-based solution for early intervention in age related macular degeneration (AMD) to prevent disease progression
text:
This research addresses the urgent need for early intervention in intermediate age-related macular
degeneration (iAMD), a major cause of vision loss among the elderly, affecting millions of Americans. The de-
velopment of our novel gene therapy, OCLX-001, aims to prevent the progression of iAMD to the more severe
stages, enhancing quality of life and reducing associated healthcare costs. By restoring and maintaining cellular
function in the retina, our approach has the potential to fundamentally alter the management of AMD, delivering
a much-needed solution to lengthen effective vision and reduce the burden of blindness in the aging population.

title: Alternative Perioperative Strategies to Control Cerebral Edema
text:
Brain tumor patients are usually given a steroid called dexamethasone (Dex) before and after surgery to reduce
brain swelling, but new evidence shows it may weaken the immune system and make treatments like radiation
and immunotherapy less effective. This study will test whether it is safe to avoid using Dex and whether a different
drug, Azeliragon, can control brain swelling without harming the immune system. If successful, this research
could change how brain tumors are treated, helping patients respond better to therapy and live longer.

title: Brain Mechanisms Mediating Genetic Risk for Anxiety and Depression
text:
New treatments for anxiety disorders are critically needed and a more complete understanding of pathological
anxiety at the molecular, cellular and circuit levels will provide a foundation for new treatment development.
Using our non-human primate model of extreme anxiety, the proposed studies will use neuroimaging, molecular
sequencing techniques and chemogenetics to understand the extent to which neurons in the dorsolateral
prefrontal cortex are involved in the expression of early-life pathological anxiety and could serve as treatment
targets for anxiety disorders. Additionally, these studies will serve as a proof-of-concept to understand the
feasibility of developing chemogenetic approaches for the modulation of prefrontal cortical function in the
treatment of severe and refractory psychiatric disorders.

title: A blind source separation approach for deconvolution of bulk transcriptional data leads to early detection of ATF cell-states in complex bacterial populations, in vitro and in vivo
text: SUMMARY – PROJECT 3 Transient bacterial cell-states including tolerance, persistence and hetero-resistance (HR) are harbingers of antibiotic treatment failure (ATF) and enablers of antibiotic resistance. Importantly, they are missed in any currently employed diagnostic assay or antibiotic susceptibility tests. Intriguingly, in the treatment of different types of cancer, physicians are often confronted with similar treatment failure issues. It turns out that these epigenetic cell-states create extended opportunities for high-level resistance mutations to emerge. Moreover, due to the phenotype’s transience, they themselves can directly drive the re-emergence of the (susceptible) population after drug pressure subsides. While these cell-states are increasingly recognized as drivers that sit at the root of treatment failure, new strategies are emerging to specifically identify, track and target them. To achieve such highly targeted treatment, approaches are developed that map out the composition of complex cancer tissue, for instance through single cell RNA-Seq (scRNA-Seq), or computational deconvolution of bulk RNA-Seq data. While, scRNA-Seq on bacteria remains technically challenging we found that by modifying existing tools, specific bacterial cell-states can be identified in complex bacterial populations. However, the capabilities of current tools are limited, and through the implementation of state-of-the-art machine learning algorithms there is much room for improvement. Moreover, ATF cell-states are poorly characterized, making it currently impossible to effectively define them. Herein, 3 aims are pursued to develop an approach that, based on bulk RNA-Seq data, dissects a complex bacterial population into its separate cell-states, and calculates their frequencies and MICs. In Aim 1 a large and diverse temporal RNA-Seq dataset is generated by following a wide variety of strains and species while they are exposed to antibiotics and a subset of the population switches to an ATF cell state. In Aim 2 a blind source separation algorithm is explored to design a state-of-the-art machine learning tool that deconvolves bulk RNA-Seq data from a complex bacterial population into the cell-states and their frequencies that make up the population. Moreover, by reconstituting each cell-state’s expression profile we enable transcriptional entropy calculations and thereby cell-state specific MIC predictions. In Aim 3 the approach is validated by retrospectively predicting the presence of ATF cell-states in patient samples. Finally, the model’s applicability is extended to bulk dual RNA-Seq data from host and bacterium, and validated on patient serum samples. This project therefore not only informs on how ATF cell-states develop and are maintained in a population, but also creates a path towards the development of diagnostics that can detect them in an active infection. Combined with the collateral sensitivities from Project 2 this could eventually enable linking detection to targeted treatment decisions.

title: Advancing statistical genetics tools for reliable drug target discovery and treatment optimization
text:
This program aims to develop and apply advanced statistical genetics tools to overcome methodological
challenges in characterizing the potential causal effects of circulating proteins and metabolites on complex
diseases. These innovations will facilitate the discovery of novel drug targets, optimize therapeutic regimens,
and enable precision treatment strategies, ultimately improving health outcomes across diverse populations.

title: Development of an mHealth intervention to reduce substance use and HIV risk for young adult women affected by sex trafficking
text:
Sex trafficking has known adverse health effects that affect young adult women disproportionally due to a wide
gap in available state and federally-funded health and social services. The proposed study will utilize
qualitative and ecological momentary assessment (EMA) methods to establish the needs of young adult
women affected by sex trafficking, available resources, and complex determinants that contribute to HIV risk
and substance use. Findings will guide the development of an mHealth intervention that will include resource
and just-in-time adaptive intervention (JITAI) components, which will be tested in a two-group pilot randomized
controlled trial.

title: Perivascular tissue models to overcome MGMT-mediated temozolomide resistance in glioblastoma
text:
Glioblastoma is the most aggressive and deadly form of brain cancer whose poor clinical outcome stems from
its diffuse invasion throughout the brain and drug resistance. This project will develop and thoroughly
characterize a tissue engineering platform to investigate pathophysiological processes responsible for invasive
spreading, therapeutic resistance, and poor survival.

title: Identifying how alcohol-evoked changes in neural firing affect systems level computations during decision-making
text:
The proposed project will advance our understanding of how changes in brain cell function relate to
malfunctioning decision-making in alcohol use disorder. The results of this research will guide future studies that
seek to develop new treatments for people with or at risk of developing alcohol use disorder.

title: BCCMA: Basic and Translational Mechanisms of Cancer Initiation of the Urothelium in Veterans Exposed to Carcinogens: Leveraging Artificial Neural Networks to Enhance Detection of Carcinoma in situ
text:
Bladder cancer is the fourth most prevalent cancer among Veterans. Carcinoma in situ (CIS) of the bladder
is a pre-invasive lesion caused by carcinogens in tobacco smoke, occupational exposures to hazardous
chemicals, and chemical/biologic warfare. CIS has a high rate of recurrence and progression to invasion and
metastasis. CIS is a major diagnostic challenge and up to 40% of CIS are missed by standard cystoscopy.
Current approved cystoscopy technologies have significant shortcomings, particularly high false positive
rates. We aim to leverage artificial intelligence to augment enhanced cystoscopy imaging technologies to
improve real-time cystoscopic detection and characterization of CIS. We propose three specific aims: 1) to
develop an annotated multimodal cystoscopy imaging dataset for CIS of the bladder; 2) to develop and train
deep learning algorithms for detection of CIS of the bladder; and 3) to augment detection of CIS of the bladder
using deep learning algorithms in clinical settings.

title: Impact of microbiota on AIDS-Kaposi’s sarcoma development and therapy
text:
Kaposi’s sarcoma-associated herpesvirus (KSHV) causes several human cancers including Kaposi’s
sarcoma, the most common cancer in AIDS patients. KSHV infection and Kaposi’s sarcoma inflict morbidity
and mortality to the society in US and worldwide, which particularly affect underrepresented people living with
HIV (PLWH) and cancer. This project will identify the factors that contribute to the development and
therapeutic outcome of Kaposi’s sarcoma, thus providing the scientific basis for developing novel prevention
and treatment approaches to benefit the patients.

title: Plasticity and Nitric Oxide Signaling: Identifying the Novel Adaptive Mechanisms Associated with Response to Hypoxia
text:
The objective of this project is to prepare Dr. Allie Graham to transition to a position as an independent, tenure-
track academic investigator. This project focuses on identifying convergent mechanisms in the adaptation to
hypoxia in high-altitude mammal lineages, and also utilizes zebrafish as a model for hypoxia response to
specifically probe the roles of nitric-oxide signaling in hypoxia acclimatization, as well as understanding how
hypoxia exposure during development primes future response, both in the adult and in its offspring. This
proposal represents an opportunity to improve our understanding of which mechanisms hypoxia-adapted
lineages use to mitigate the long-term detrimental physiological effects of long-term hypoxia exposure, like
pulmonary hypertension, erythrocytosis/polycythemia, and cardiovascular disease.

title: Resting and Dynamic Brain Glutamate by MRS In Vivo: Relation to Suicidal Behavior
text:
Rising suicide fatality rates in the US underscore the need to identify novel and effective therapeutic targets
for suicide risk, beyond existing monoamine-focused treatments such as antidepressants. Evidence
suggests that glutamatergic neurotransmission is important to the pathophysiology of suicide. This project
will assess alterations in brain glutamatergic signaling both at rest and during task-related activity
in depressed individuals at risk for suicidal behavior.

title: Function of Zymogen Granule 16B (ZG16B) in Salivary Glands
text:
Salivary proteome analysis could identify risk factors of the salivary gland tissues in chronic oral inflammatory
conditions such as chronic graft-versus-host disease (cGVHD) and lichenoid lesions (including oral lichen
planus). Recently, our lab quantified a decrease in the salivary levels of zymogen granule 16B (ZG16B), a
jacalin-related lectin protein, in the saliva of cGVHD observed in survivors of allogeneic hematopoietic stem
transplants (HSCT). This project aims to further elucidate the functional consequences of ZG16B through the
changes in saliva content of ZG16B (healthy vs. oral inflammatory conditions), identify relevant protein-protein
binding partners and contributions to cell signaling pathways.

title: Quantitative Light Microscopy Shared Resource
text: The Quantitative Light Microscopy Shared Resource (QLMSR – formerly known as the Live Cell Imaging Shared Resource) of the Simmons Comprehensive Cancer Center (SCCC) enables SCCC members to leverage state- of-the-art light microscopy techniques in support of their cancer-focused research. QLMSR capabilities include digital imaging of histologically stained samples, laser-scanning and spinning disk confocal microscopy, two- photon microscopy for imaging in live animals and thick tissues, total internal reflection fluorescence (TIRF) microscopy, and multiple modes of super-resolution imaging, as well as three image processing workstations with comprehensive image analysis software. Led by the QLMSR Director, the shared resource staff consults on experimental design, experimental goals, and sample preparation, then advises on the optimal imaging platform to use and provides individualized training of users on any given system. Finally, the QLMSR helps with image quantification and automation of analysis as needed. To stay at the forefront of technology, QLMSR has been proactive in constantly evaluating new instrumentation and in obtaining funding for the purchase of cutting-edge hardware and software. Since 2020, based on user feedback and usage analysis, QLMSR has expanded its capacity by adding two spinning disk confocal microscopes – one funded through the NIH S10 program (S10OD028630) – as well as one laser scanning confocal microscope. Latter imaging platform is a Zeiss LSM980 with Airyscan-2 attachment for “one-click" super resolution imaging, an optical configuration that allows imaging in the near infrared spectrum, as well as a fluorescence correlation spectroscopy module for examining molecular interactions in solution and in living cells. To enable the use of highly specialized imaging modalities, QLMSR partners with various UT Southwestern (UTSW) departments to provide expertise in, and access to, additional imaging platforms, including a 'facility line STED microscope' (Aberrior), an 'ImageXpress confocal HT.ai' high- content imaging system (Molecular devices), as well as custom-build light sheet microscopes. These platforms are made available to SCCC members through the QLMSR. Since 2020, QLMSR has been used by principal investigators across all five SCCC research programs, resulting in 141 cancer-focused manuscripts, including publications in Cell, Nature, Science, Cancer Cell, Nature Communications, Developmental Cell, and Nature Microbiology. The number of SCCC member laboratories using the QLMSR has been steady since 2020 and ranges from 74 to 92 on a yearly basis, yet, with the addition of new imaging platforms, the hourly usage per year of QLMSR's equipment and services has doubled, from 4,432 hrs in 2021 (similar to pre-Covid usage) to 8,987 hrs in 2024. This significant increase is largely due to the expansion of QLMSR’s hardware resources, a strong increase in autonomous use, as well as an increase in projects that require long-term (overnight) imaging sessions. Overall, the extensive usage of the QLMSR highlights the great value and importance of this SR in support of cancer-focused research.

title: Computer-aided design and development of isoform selective inhibitors of Casein Kinase 1
text:
Off-target effects by therapeutic agents are mainly connected to the toxicity of current drug candidates in
clinical studies, while achieving specific inhibition of the desired target of interest is a challenging task due to
the high degree of similarity among enzymes inside cells. We propose a research plan that combines
computational studies, multi-step synthesis, biochemical assay, and structural biology to systematically
investigate a family of enzymes and to identify distinct structural features in enzymes of interest. This research
will provide new insights into specific inhibition mechanisms for targets of interest, and it aims to produce highly
specific chemical agents that may be further developed to new therapeutic candidates.

title: Mapping the cell-type-specific molecular and genetic basis of lupus using single cell multiomics
text:
Systemic lupus erythematosus (SLE) is a chronic autoimmune disease with variable presentation of symptoms
and inconsistent response to therapy. Here, we propose to use highly innovative single cell epigenomic,
transcriptomic, and proteomic analyses to map the cell-type-specific molecular and genetic basis underlying SLE
heterogeneity. We expect our findings to shed light on the pathogenic states in specific immune cell subsets
stratifying SLE patients, which, in turn, will create new opportunities for therapies directed toward each specific
patient subgroup.
2

title: Investigating The Role of The Human Mannose Receptor (CD206) During M. tuberculosis Infection in a Novel Transgenic Mouse
text:
The mannose receptor (MR), a pattern recognition receptor (PRR) abundantly expressed on alveolar
macrophages (AMs), mediates phagocytosis of Mycobacterium tuberculosis (M.tb) but paradoxically facilitates
intracellular bacterial growth and survival. Using a novel transgenic mouse model that exclusively expresses the
human MR (hMR), this project will investigate hMR-mediated downstream signaling during TB pathogenesis.
These studies will enhance our understanding of species-specific differences in MR signaling and immune
response and may reveal novel targets for HDT against TB and other airborne infectious agents.

title: WashU Somatic Mosaicism across Human Tissues (SMaHT) Program Organizational Center
text:
The WashU Somatic Mosaicism across Human Tissues Program Organizational Center (SMaHT-OC) will
serve as the nucleus for facilitating all activities of the SMaHT Network. We will define rules and mechanisms of
communication, will empower researchers to engage with multimodal "big bio-data", and will provide
administrative and budget support for developing and managing engagement and training. Through innovative
methodology, we will establish a research environment that promotes collaboration, coordination, and
communication among SMaHT Network participants and the scientific community.
.

title: Precision Approaches to Reduce Asthma Disparities with Electronic Health Record Data
text:
Asthma, a chronic lung disease that affects 20 million American adults, has well-known disparities in prevalence,
severity and death by race/ethnicity, socioeconomic status and sex. We will use Electronic Health Record (EHR)
data enhanced with information on social, economic, and environmental characteristics to identify sub-groups of
adults with asthma who share common patterns of risk factors. This information will be used to create a tool that
can support precision patient care strategies, as well as motivate public health strategies to decrease asthma risk
in specific geographic areas.
